glossary.definition: A 100 megabit-per-second local area network known by the generic name of Fast Ethernet operating over twisted-pair copper cable. This technology is becoming very popular and cost-effective. It is designed to integrate with existing networks with minimal disruption.
A twisted-pair cable version of an IEEE 802.3 network.

An XFP is a hot-pluggable compact transceiver used for data communications and telecommunications. It interfaces a so-called “parent board” to a fiber optic. The XFP layout has been standardized by a consortium of leading suppliers of telecommunications equipment. XFP is protocol independent, can support OC-192/STM-64, 10 Gigabit Ethernet, 10 Gigabit Fibre Channel, and ITU-T G.709 data streams in routers, switches and network cards. Reaches ranging from Very Short Reach (VSR) to Long Reach (LR) can also be supported.

A protection architecture in which the transmitting equipment transmits a valid signal on both the working and protection lines. The receiving equipment monitors both lines. Based on performance criteria and OS control, the receiving equipment chooses one line as the active line and designates the other as the standby line.

Optical noise generated in an erbium-doped fiber amplifier (EDFA) with and without signal input power.
A device that converts analog signals into digital signals.
A 5° 15° angle on the connector tip for the minimum possible back reflection.
Loss at a connector caused by misaligned fiber end-face angles. Anomaly

The smallest observable discrepancy between the actual and the necessary characteristic of a system component. The occurrence of a single anomaly does not interrupt the ability to perform a required function. Anomalies do not result in any consequent actions, but are contributors to defects and performance monitoring counts.
Agence Nationale de la Sécurité des Systèmes d’Information, a French governmental agency in charge of qualifying the security rules.
Agence Nationale de la Sécurité des Systèmes d’Information (National Agency for the Security of Information) Qualification Standard
A thin dielectric or metallic film applied to an optical surface to reduce its reflection and thereby increase its transmission.
ASCII name assigned by the manufacturer to identify a particular card by card type and number.
Application Software License Management generates the pool key files from the customer-purchased licenses from the ordering systems.
Gathering together of payload data with overhead and pointer information (an indication of the direction of the signal).
A logical connection between manager and agent through which management information can be exchanged.
Data that is transmitted without an associated clock signal
An Optical Transport Network (OTN) mapping method using asynchronous mapping with dedicated stuff byte positions in the ODU server layer AMP is also used to denote an amplifier
The decrease in signal strength along a fiber optic waveguide caused by absorption and scattering. Attenuation is usually expressed in dB/km.
A passive device that reduces the amplitude of a signal without distorting the waveform.
Alarm indication level: critical, major, minor, or no alarm.
Configuration of system parts without preprovisioning. When a part is plugged into the system, it is accepted with its default configuration.

Action taken by the system in the event of card failure/trouble. System switches to protection and prevents a return to the working card even if the trouble clears. Multiple protection switches on a card during a short period of time cause the system to autolock the card.

One possible state of a port or slot. When a port is in the AINS state and a good signal is detected, the port automatically enters the IS (in-service) state. When a port or slot is in the AINS state and a card is detected, the slot/port automatically enters the IS state. The important things about AINS state is that alarms are suppressed. Absence of the card is not alarmed. Absence of a signal is not alarmed on the port.

The lowering of the laser power to a limit that fits into the class 1 category for handling fiber cables. APR replaces the full power-off feature known as ALS (automatic laser shutdown) or APSD (automatic power shutdown).
A technique (procedure) to automatically shutdown the output power of optical amplifiers to avoid exposure to hazardous levels.
A protection switch that occurs automatically in response to an automatically detected fault condition.
An optical network that is able to automatically manage signalling and routing.

Message sent by the system to the CIT to notify it of any state change in the system. Autonomous messages are not responses to a CIT-initiated command. Examples of these messages include alarms, events (non-alarmed condition), notification of connections that are added or deleted, and changes in the system database.
An autonomous TL1 message (event) counter used to detect lost events.

A photodetector that can be regarded as the semiconductor analog to photomultipliers. By applying a high reverse bias voltage (typically 100-200 V in silicon), an APD shows an internal current gain effect (around 100) due to impact ionization (avalanche effect).
See “Fresnel reflection” (p. 1602) for definition.
Errors identified through OTN performance monitoring.
The return of a portion of scattered light to the input end of a fiber; the scattering of light in the direction opposite to its original propagation.
The OT port has detected a Backward Defect Indication at the ODUk Path layer. This defect indicates that the peer OTUk port has detected condition that is treated as Server Signal Failure
Indicates the OMS or OTS overhead signal fail status detection in the OMS or OTS termination sink function.
Indicates the OMS or OTS payload signal fail status detection in the OMS or OTS termination sink function.
Signal that indicates the count of interleaved-bit blocks that have been detected in error in the upstream direction.
The difference in Hz between the highest and lowest frequencies in a transmission channel. The data rate that can be carried by a provided communications circuit.

The range of frequencies supported for all the channels on a link, from the lowest channel edge supported to the highest channel edge supported. For WS-P, this range varies per DWDM link in the network. Only DWDM-FLEX link types support extended ranges, if the design uses the hardware that support that range.
Transmission rate of data (bits per second) on a network link.
Battery Distribution Fuse Board
The smallest radius an optical fiber or fiber cable can bend before increased attenuation or breakage occurs

An algorithm specified in IEEE Std 1588 to help select the best time source of a PTP clock. It compares datasets describing two PTP timeTransmitter clocks to determine the dataset that describe the better one and whether the next recommended state of the PTP ports will be TIME_TRANSMITTER, TIME_ RECEIVER, or PASSIVE based on the results of BTCA. The BTCA is composed of two separate algorithm: • Dataset comparison algorithm • State decision algorithm ITU-T G.8275.1 telecom PTP profile uses an Alternate BTCA (ABTCA). The ABTCA slightly differs from the default BTCA of IEEE 1588 (optimized for telecom topologies and supporting multiple Grandmasters).
A transmission path consisting of two fibers that handle traffic in both the transmit and receive directions.

A survivable SONET transport architecture that protects against cable cuts and node failures by providing duplicate, geographically diverse paths for each service. Network elements are interconnected in a closed fiber loop (four fibers for a four-fiber BLSR architecture or two fibers for a two-fiber BLSR). A service can reach its destination by traveling in either direction around the ring. Exactly one-half of the bandwidth available between adjacent nodes in each direction is used for working traffic, with the remaining bandwidth available for protection.
Protection switching performed in both the transmit and receive directions.
BER measures how accurately a bitstream is transmitted through a system. It measures how many bits are received in error, compared to how many bits are sent.
A method of error monitoring over a specified number of bits (BIP-3 or BIP-8).
A method of mapping a client signal for transport across the Optical Transport Network (OTN).

A small module (printed wiring board plus components) that plugs into almost every card (other than the NCTL, SCTL, and SUPVY) to supply the processor, memory, and intra-NE communications capabilities required to operate the card in the system.
Binary Phase Shift Keying.
The setting up of a cross-connection leg with the same input tributary as that of an existing cross- connection leg, therefore forming a 1:2 bridge from an input tributary to two output tributaries.
Voice, data, and/or video communications at greater than 2 Mbit/s rates.
STM-1 concatenation transport over the 1830 Photonic Service Switch for ATM applications.
A method for distributing a precision clock among telecommunications equipment.
A CFP is a pluggable optical module with either 40 or 100 Gb/s transmission rate. The CFP layout has been standardized by a consortium of leading suppliers of telecommunications equipment.
A cable that is connector-terminated and ready for installation.
Consists of all the optical elements including fiber connectors and splices between a transmitter and a receiver.

glossary.term: Carrier Sense Multiple Access with Collision Detection (CSMA/CD)
glossary.definition: A control technique for getting onto and off a LAN. All devices attached to the network listen for transmissions in progress (that is, carrier sense) before starting to transmit (multiple access). If two or more begin transmitting at the same time and their transmissions crash into each other, each backs off (collision detection ) for a different amount of time (determined by an algorithm) before again attempting to transmit.
See “Clear Channel” (p. 1591) for definition. See “Cross-connection” (p. 1593) for definition.

glossary.term: CCITT (Consultative Committee for the International Telephone and Telegraph)
glossary.definition: See “International Telecommunication Union-Telecommunications Sector ” (p. 1605) for definition.

In a laser, the nominal value central operating wavelength. It is the wavelength defined by a peak mode measurement where the effective optical power resides. In a LED, the average of the two wavelengths measured at the half-amplitude points of the power spectrum.

A CO can be a building, a switch, or collection of switches where subscriber lines are joined to switching equipment that connects the subscribers to each other, other subscribers, and/or long-distance subscribers.
Carrier Ethernet Switch Router, for example, Nokia 7450 ESS
A measure of how much air moves through the fan of air-coded equipment.
A sub-unit of transmission capacity within a defined higher level of transmission capacity.
COF cards facilitate the WaveKey encoding function, employed at service endpoints.

A multiple of 12.5 GHz, is the width of the bandwidth allotted to the WS-P trail signal at an OADM, width can vary along the path as the hardware constraints and center frequency chosen require. Currently, the only width values supported are 50, 62.5, and 75 GHz, even on DWDM-100 GHz link types.
In laser diodes, the shift of the lasers central wavelength during single-pulse duration caused by laser instability.

The speed that an optical pulse travels depends on the fiber wavelength. This speed is caused by several factors including material dispersion, waveguide dispersion, and profile dispersion. The net effect of chromatic dispersion is that if an optical pulse contains multiple wavelengths (colors), then the different colors travel at different speeds and arrive at different times, spreading the received optical signal.
A set of transmission channels through one or more network elements that provides transmission of signals between two points, to support a single communications path.
Comité International Spécial des Perturbations Radioélectriques

Material that surrounds the core of an optical fiber that has a lower index of refraction compared to that of the core. The lower index of refraction causes the transmitted light to travel down the core.

Routing for networks of variable sizes, defined by a variable-length subnet mask. By using subnet mask values other than 255 (all ones) for a particular octet, the bits in the network address that are not covered by the subnet mask can be sized to create networks that do not conform to the original Class A, B, and C subnet definitions.
A digital circuit where no framing or control bits are required, therefore making the full bandwidth available for communications.

COMMON LANGUAGE equipment code. Used by network service providers for inventory, engineering, spare piece-part ordering, provisioning and maintenance operations. CLEI codes identify the specific form, fit and function of equipment items used network topologies.
A client is a computer, device or program that requests services from a network. Client also may refer to the terminating device at one end of a network node.
Alarm indication of a client signal failure

A technique used in Local Area Networks (LANs) whereby a data octet is subdivided, scrambled, and encoded into an expanded form. The expanded expression of the data value includes bits that are used for clock recovery.
A network formed of a ring-shaped configuration of network elements. Each network element connects to two others, one on each side.
Coded Mark Inversion
Serialized CMISS information
A hardware configuration where two applications can be active at the same time independently on the same hardware and software platform without interfering with each others functioning.

the method of combining multiple signals on laser beams at various wavelengths for transmission along fiber optic cables. The number of channels is fewer than in dense wavelength division multiplexing (DWDM), but more than in standard wavelength division multiplexing (WDM).
Set of federal regulations for broad areas of control. Different parts relate to different industries. The telecommunication industry is related to title 47 of the CFR.
System elements that are located in the same location.
An administrator-defined group that defines commands to which a user has access.
Identifies equipment that is capable of sustaining normal operation in commercial temperature ranges, for example, 0°C to +70°C, −5°C to +70°C, or −5°C to +75°C.
Software tool for automated provisioning, commissioning and power balancing functions of photonic networks based on the 1830 PSS portfolio of WDM products.

A procedure whereby multiple virtual containers are associated one with each other resulting in a combined capacity that can be used as a single container across which bit sequence integrity is maintained.
Subsystem that configures the network and processes messages from the network.
A mechanical or optical device that provides a demountable connection between two fibers or a fiber and a source or detector.
Constant Bit RateType of service that provides a constant bit data transfer rate. Used for delay-intensive service such as voice or video.
The constant optical output from an optical source when it is turned on, but not modulated with a signal.

The portion of the network that carries control and management traffic (for example, communications between the NEs and between the NEs and the EMS). The control network does not carry user traffic. The control communications use the SNMP protocol.
Portion of the network or system that enables control of communication sessions and services. See also “GMPLS control plane region” (p. 1603).

IP routing performed by an NE for RSVP notify messages, and for management traffic. OSPF is used as routing protocol. A CPR domain contains NEs and Network Operation Centers (NOCs). CPR domains can be de-coupled from IP routing in the operators DCN, by setting up IP-in-IP tunnels between NEs attached to the Out-of-band DCN, and NOCs.
The central portion of the fiber that transmits light. It is composed of material with a higher index of refraction than the cladding.
A user supplied label attached to an input command that is repeated in the associated response to facilitate the correlation of input to response.
An optical device that combines or splits power from optical fibers.
The ratio/loss of optical power from one output port to the total output power, expressed as a percentage.
Alarm that indicates a severe, service-affecting condition.

A local interface between the user and a unit that is used to issue commands to the local system or to log in remotely to another system on the same fiber as the local system. Cross-connection (CC ) (XC ) Path-level connections between input and output tributaries or specific ports within a single NE. Cross- connections are made in a consistent way even though there are various types of ports and various types of port protection. Cross-connections are reconfigurable interconnections between tributaries of transmission interfaces.
An unwanted signal introduced into one transmission line from another.
Clock Recovery Unit
The whole software and (static) data presently associated with a particular NE release.
The value currently assigned to a provisionable parameter.
Terminal and associated equipment and inside wiring located at a subscribers premises. The equipment is connected with the carriers communication network at the demarcation point.
An 8 port colorless wavelength router; 44-channel capacity.
An 8 port colorless wavelength router; 88-channel capacity.
A method to detect erroneous bits in a byte stream.
Destination access point identifier
A collection of system parameters and their associated values.
A portion of the SDH/SONET signal that contains alarm, surveillance, and performance information.
A configuration of telecommunications equipment for the purpose of transmitting data rather than analog signals.
The equipment that originates data for transmission and accepts transmitted data.
A user who administers the database of the application.
A databearer represents a physical link connection between two nodes in the transport plane.
Data Center Connect See also“Data Communication Channel” (p. 1596) for definition.
An operation or value that the system or application assumes, unless a user makes an explicit choice.
The parameter values that are preprogrammed as shipped from the factory.
A limited interruption of the ability of an item to perform a required function. It may or may not lead to maintenance action depending on the results of additional analysis.
Identification of signal delay between measurement points.
A device that splits a combined signal into individual signals at the receiver end of transmission.
A process applied to a multiplexed signal for recovering signals combined within it and for restoring the distinct individual channels of these signals.

A multiplexing technique that uses close spectral spacing of individual optical carrier wavelengths to reduce the total number of fibers required to provide a specific amount of information-carrying capacity. The technique takes advantage of desirable transmission characteristics (for example, minimum dispersion or attenuation) within a provided fiber.
The inverse order of provisioning. To manually remove/delete a parameter that has (or parameters that have) previously been provisioned.
In an optical fiber, the variation in propagation delay that occurs because of the different group velocities of different modes.
A field in an IP packet that enables different levels of service to be assigned to network traffic.
Equipment that combines by time-division multiplexing several digital signals into a single composite digital signal.
A transmission span such as an STM- N signal. A digital section may contain multiple digital channels.
A digital signaling rate of 1.544 Mb/s.
A digital signal rate of 44.736 Mb/s
A specialized semiconductor device that converts analog signals into digital signals.
A device that converts digital signals into analog signals.
A coupling device for separately sampling (through a known coupling loss) either the forward (incident) or the backward (reflected) wave in a transmission line.
An operating system application process that provides the directory functionality.
Splitting up a signal into its constituents as payload data and overhead (an indication of the direction of a signal).
The temporal spreading of a light signal in an optical waveguide caused by light signals traveling at different speeds through a fiber either due to modal or chromatic effects.
A special fiber with a negative chromatic dispersion coefficient used to compensate the positive chromatic dispersion of the transmission fiber in the third optical window.
Spooled fiber used to control excess dispersion found in certain fiber types at pre- and post-amplification.
A technique that allows solitons to become more resistant to errors when they are propagating inside optical fibers.
The difference in value between two measurements of a signal (transmitted and received).
When there is unequal amplification of incoming wavelengths, the result is a power divergence between wavelengths.
See “Delay Measurement” (p. 1596) for definition. See “Dispersion Management” (p. 1597) for definition.
Do Not Use
The addition of impurities to a substance in order to attain required properties.
Two shelves with a fan assembly between them and a heat baffle below the lower shelf.
At or toward the destination of the considered transmission stream, for example, looking in the same direction of transmission.
Data Plane Routing

A circuit configuration that provides redundant signal appearances at the outputs of two network elements in a ring. Can be used for Dual Node Ring Interworking (DNI) and for video distribution applications.
A topology where two rings are interconnected at two nodes on each ring and operate so that inter-ring traffic is not lost in the event of a node or link failure at an interconnecting point.
Do not USe
A filter that equalizes the gain of an optical signal.
Device that flattens the output spectrum of an Erbium-Doped Fiber Amplifier (EDFA).
DHCP allows a DHCP server to automatically assign an IP address to a computers TCP/IP stack software. The number is taken from a defined range of numbers for a provided network.
Electrical Subnetwork Connection Protection
Ethernet-based communication network
Embedded Communication Channel

glossary.term: Electrically Erasable and Programmable Read-Only Memory (EEPROM)
glossary.definition: A kind of non-volatile memory often used to store inventory data.
A measure of equipment tolerance to external electromagnetic fields.
High-energy, electrically induced magnetic fields that cause data corruption in cables passing through the fields.
An organization composed as an alliance of trade associations for electronics manufacturers in the United States. It establishes electrical and functional standards.

eVOAs control optical power leveling through software provisioning. Works with the Tap module to provide input for Wavelength Tracker modulation and provides optical tap for feedback signal to the Wavelength Tracker.
ESD The spontaneous transfer of electrostatic charge.
System that manages NEs either directly attached to it or are remotely connected by using the DCN. Examples of these systems are the WebUI and NMS.
Optical equipment that terminates optical line signals.
Defines the status or values at the end of the guaranteed lifetime of a component. EOL is reached when the wear-out failure rate dominates the component failure rate.

A software tool for automated design and planning of photonic networks based on the 1830 PSS portfolio of WDM products. EPT is no longer supported, WaveSuite Planner (WS-P) replaces the 1830 EPT product.

A set of rules that determine the system configuration possibilities based on fiber type, OA, rate, and number of wavelengths. These rules also determine the maximum loss per span that can be tolerated, the maximum distance between spans allowed, and the maximum number of spans that can be supported.
A specific piece of hardware (usually a card, slot, or module) that has been assigned a name recognized by the system.
The name used by the system to refer to a card, memory device, or communications link.
End of Sequence

In addition to system processing and communication for the shelf, the Equipment Controller module provides monitors the status of active and standby modules, maintains a database of all cards installed in the shelf, supports communications interfaces and LED indicators on the User Interface Panel, and communicates with extension shelves. Equipment Protection Switching (EPS ) (EQPS ) Feature that restores equipment by switching over to redundant services.
Optical fibers doped with the rare earth element erbium that can amplify light in the 1550 nm region when pumped by an external light source.

A performance monitoring parameter. ES “type A” is a second with exactly one error; ES “type B” is a second with more than one and less than the number of errors in a severely errored second for the provided signal. ES by itself means the sum of the type A and type B ESs.
Electrostatic Protection
Ethernet Services Switch
A user-initiated command, at the 1830 PSS ZIC , to create an entity and its associated attributes in the absence of certain hardware.
Ethernet MAC (Layer 2) interface. Refer to ITU-T G.8010 for more information.
Ethernet performance monitoring measurement of frame delay and frame delay variation.
Ethernet performance monitoring measurement where the frame loss is calculated based on service frame counters.
Ethernet Synthetic Loss Measurement Ethernet performance monitoring measurement where the frame loss is calculated based on synthetic frame counters.
Extended Temperature Range

European Telecommunications Standards Institute. ETSI is the European counterpart to ANSI. Its task is to pave the way for telecommunications integration in the European community as part of the single European market program. It establishes telecommunication standards for the European community.
Ethernet PHY layer interface. Refer to ITU-T G.8010 and IEEE 802.3 for more information.
A German acronym that stands for “Europaïsche Norm”.

A significant change. Events in controlled Network Elements include signal failures, equipment failures, signals exceeding thresholds, and protection switch activity. When an event occurs in a controlled Network Element, the controlled Network Element will generate an alarm or status message and send it to the management system.
The calculated average bit error rate over a data stream.
“experimental use” bits in the MPLS packet header, defined in IETF RFC 3032 and renamed in IETF RFC 5462 as the “Traffic Class” field.
When laser is modulated using a Mach-Zehnder modulator.
The ratio of two optical powers of a digital signal generated by an optical source.
Unprotected traffic that is carried over protection channels when their capacity is not used for the protection of working traffic.
Full-Function CRU (Clock Recovery Unit)
The part of an optical system that is responsible for switching voice, data, or video from one place to another.
Protection schemes that involve switching traffic from a failed facility to a standby (protection) facility.
A unit of failure rate in reliability analysis. One FIT is equivalent to one failure per one billion operating hours.
The number of failures of a device per unit of time.

The time required for the trailing edge of a pulse to fall from 90% to 10% of its amplitude; the time required for a component to produce such a result. Typically measured between the 80% and 20% points or the 90% and 10% points. Also called turn-off time.
Any other network element in a maintenance subnetwork other than the one the user is at or working on. Also called remote.
An indication returned to the transmitting node that an errored block has been detected at the receiving node. A block is a specified grouping of bits.
An indication returned to a transmitting Network Element that the receiving Network Element has detected an incoming section failure. Also known as RDI.

Because WaveTracker (WT) encoding requires a faster frequency response, fVOAs are required for WT keying. fVOAs modulate the power of the frequency to keep tone. WT keying enables the customer to identify a channel downstream because the frequency is known and the system can identify the modulation depth (amplitude of the modulation) of the channel power.
Term used when a card or signal has a hard (not temporary) fault and cannot perform its normal function. For signals the fault may be temporary.
Collecting, processing, and forwarding of autonomous messages from network elements.
A special curved polish on the connector for very low back reflection.
Federal Communications Commission. The U.S. federal regulatory agency responsible for the regulation of interstate and international communications by radio, television, wire, satellite, and cable.
The Food and Drug Administrations Center for Devices and Radiological Health.
A rigid tube that confines or holds a fiber as part of a connector assembly.
Fixed gain optical amplifier module (+16 dBm power, 18-dB gain).
A cable containing one or more optical fibers. Fiber Optic
A threaded optical connector for single-mode or multimode fiber and applications requiring low back reflection.
A user-configurable logic device that holds user-defined logic constructs and interconnects in the form of a microprocessor. Examples include EEPROM and FLASH.

A protocol used for exchanging files over the Internet. FTP uses the Internet TCP/IP protocols to enable data transfer. FTP is most commonly used to download/upload a file to/from a server using the Internet.

Card that provides functions such as communications between the NE and the managing system and/or neighboring NE, Debug LAN access for service personnel, management interfaces, and management agents including event reporting and logging, equipment database management, software download and management, performance monitoring management, alarm management, and security management.
The number of device failures in one billion device hours.
Type of OADM where the wavelength arrangement scheme can only input or output a single wavelength via the fixed port.

glossary.term: Fixed-rate tributary operation of a port
glossary.definition: Mode of operation of a port in which tributaries are provisioned for the expected signal rates. This provisioning information is used for cross-connection rate validation and for alarm handling (for example “Loss of Pointer”).

Supported with WS-P link types DWDM-50 GHz and DWDM-100 GHz. This feature defines a line/link with channels centered on the legacy (pre-R9.1) 50 GHz/100 GHz grid. Includes only up to 88-channel support.
A nonvolatile memory device used to store the installation software generic or the NE database.
A technology that combines the non-volatility of EPROM with the in-circuit reprogrammability of EEPROM.

Supported with WS-P link type DWDM-FLEX. Line/link with channels centered on a 6.25 GHz grid, that is 6.25 GHz increments from the reference frequency 193.100 THz (193.1THz + n × 6.25GHz, were n is a positive or negative integer, including 0.) Currently, Flexgrid is supported in networks with a mix of DCM and DCM-free. The Flexgrid definition is from ITU’s G694.1 G694.1. This term does not imply anything about the bandwidth range.
Folded (collapsed) rings are rings without fiber diversity. The terminology derives from the image of folding a ring into a linear segment.
Term used when a card (either working or protection) has been locked into a service-providing state by user command.

An automatic and fully distributed capability that indicates a failure in a server networking layer (for example, Physical Layer). When used with other mechanisms such as CV (Connectivity Verification), it can indicate defects such as misbranching of LSPs and errors in swapping LSP label.

An error correction technique that redundant bits are added to the payload signal enabling the receiving station to detect and correct bit errors that unavoidably occur when an optical line signal is transmitted over longer distances over an optical fiber. FEC is used to increase the transmission span length.
Also known as a forwarding table, is most commonly used in network bridging, routing, and similar functions to find the proper interface to which the input interface must forward a packet.
The smallest block of digital data being transmitted.
A sequence at the beginning of an SDH/SONET frame that detects the frame start.
An assembly of equipment units capable of housing shelves, such as a card framework.
An operating condition of a clock in which its local oscillator is not locked to an internal synchronization reference and is using no storage techniques to sustain its accuracy.
A reference set of frequencies used to denote allowed nominal central frequencies that may be used for defining channels.
A reflection of light that occurs at the air-glass interface at the ends of an optical fiber.
The increase in power and magnitude of a signal.

When erbium-doped fibers are used to amplify the light traveling through the fiber, some wavelengths are amplified more than others. A gain-flattening filter restores all wavelengths to approximately the same intensity.
General Communications Channel

A protocol suite (defined by IETF) that extends the label switching paradigm introduced in MPLS to include both packet-switched and circuit-switched networks and that provides the distributed intelligence required to build efficient and resilient multi-layer networks. For the WaveSuite Planner (WS-P), GMPLS is a region where the GMPLS CP feasibility rules must be applied (such as OTs, Nodes, and so on).
Client/server mapping scenario that provides the ability to map any client signal into any server regardless of differences in rate.
Industry standard ITU-T G.709 FEC.

Gigabit Ethernet (GbE or 1 GigE) is the various technologies for transmitting Ethernet frames at a rate of a gigabit per second (1,000,000,000 bits per second), as defined by the IEEE 802.3-2008 standard.

Corresponds to the time to wait before switching back to the timing reference. It occurs after a timing link failure has cleared. This time applies for all timing sources in a system hence the name global. This timing can be between 0 and 60 minutes, in increments of one minute.
A GMPLS region that supports the control plane engine for routing and signaling. See also “Control Plane” (p. 1594).

A transceiver that only support a single channel per fiber - typically 850 nm, 1310 nm or 1550 nm (as opposed to colored interfaces, which can support a multiplex of wavelengths). They are commonly used in point-to-point communication links.

In telecommunications, the process of separating and segregating channels, as by combing, such that the broadest channel possible can be assembled and sent across the longest practical link. The aim is to minimize de-multiplexing traffic and reshuffling it electrically.

Noise that results when equipment is grounded at points having different potentials, thereby creating an unintended current path. The dielectric properties of optical fiber provide electrical isolation that eliminates ground loops.
An unrecoverable non-symptomatic (primary) failure that causes signal impairment or interferes with critical network functions.
OSI reference model data link layer protocol.
Higher Order

An operating condition of a clock where its local oscillator is not locked to an external reference but is using storage techniques to maintain its accuracy with respect to the last known frequency comparison with a synchronization reference.
A card ready for fast, automatic placement into operation to replace an active card. It has the same signal as the service going through it, so that choice is all that is required.
High Power Connection Fuse and Alarm Panel
Input/Output
Incoming Alignment Error
Identifier
Internet Engineering Task Force

In some physically larger networks, the distance between two Add/Drop nodes may exceed the system’s single-span optical reach. In such a case, an ILA can be installed at a mid-point, thereby creating two shorter spans and boosting the signal strength before it gets too close to the noise floor.
A memory administrative state for ports. IS refers to a port that is fully monitored and alarmed.
It is unnecessary to shut down the system to upgrade it.
Also refractive index. The ratio of the velocity of light in free space to the velocity of light in a fiber material. Symbolized by n. Always greater than or equal to one.
Identifies equipment that is capable of sustaining normal operation in industrial temperature ranges, for example, 40°C to +85°C.
To physically insert a card into a slot, therefore causing a system initiated restore of an entity into service and/or creation of an entity and associated attributes.
The loss of power that results from inserting a component, such as a connector or splice, into a previously continuous path.

glossary.term: Institute of Electrical and Electronic Engineers (IEEE)
glossary.definition: Helps advance global prosperity by promoting the engineering process of creating, developing, integrating, sharing, and applying knowledge about electrical and information technologies and sciences for the benefit of humanity and the profession.

The total number of STM-1 equivalents (bidirectional) tributaries in all transmission interfaces with which a provided transmission interface shelf can be equipped at one time. The interface capacity varies with equipage.
Optical sections from a few kilometers (km) to approximately 15 km.
A system that routes/relays management information. An SDH Network Element may be a combined intermediate and end system.
The international standards and conformity assessment body for all fields of electrotechnology, including electricity and electronics.
A United Nations agency concerned with international standardization in a broad range of industrial and technical fields.

Formerly known as CCITT (Comité Consultatif International Télégraphique & Téléphonique) or International Telegraph and Telephone Consultative Committee. Develops the worldwide telecommunications standards.

The ICMP is one of the main protocols of the Internet Protocol Suite. It is used by network devices, such as routers, to send error messages indicating, for example, that a requested service is not available or that a host or router could not be reached.
A communications protocol used by hosts and adjacent routers on IP networks to establish multicast group memberships. IGMP is an integral part of IP multicast.

A developing standard for security at the network or packet processing layer of network communication. Earlier security approaches have inserted security at the application layer of the communications model. IPsec is especially useful for implementing virtual private networks and for remote user access through dial-up connection to private networks.
Network Control Protocol for IPv4.

Developed by Telcordia, standards that vendors must adhere in order to sell equipment to the Regional Bell Operating Companies (RBOCs) and the Competitive Local Exchange Carriers (CLECs).

Provides an efficient means of managing the equipment and services within a network, including creating new services, diagnosing faults, and planning for growth. It has interfaces to external systems to allow functions such as billing, service orders, and service level agreement (SLA) management.

The ratio (in dB) between the signal-to-noise ratio applied to the input of the microwave component and the signal-to-noise ratio measured at its output. NF indicates the amount of noise added to a signal by the component during normal operations. Lower noise figures indicate less degradation and better performance.
A kind of sink termination point function that does not touch SDH/SONET signals but monitors quality of service.

Any interface providing you with information on the system behavior or control. These include the equipment LEDs, user panel, 1830 PSS ZIC , office alarms, and all telemetry interfaces.

According to the ITU-T Recommendation G.709 , the ODU k is an information structure consisting of the information payload (OPU k , Optical Channel Payload Unit) and ODU k related overhead. ODU k capacities are defined for k = 0, 1, 2, 2e, 3, 3e2, and 4 where k indicates the bit rate of the client signa (1.2 Gbit/s, 2.5 Gbit/s, 10.0 Gbit/s, 10.4 Gbit/s, 40.4 Gbit/s, 41.8 Gbit/s, 104.8 Gbit/s).
Contains the encapsulated client data, and a header describing the type of that data.
The Optical Transport Unit (OTU) frame carries different traffic types—including Ethernet, storage, digital video, as well as SONET/SDH.

According to the ITU-T Recommendation G.709 , the OTUk is the information structure used for the transport of an ODU k over one or more optical channel connections. It consists of the optical channel data unit and OTU k related overhead (FEC and overhead for management of an optical channel connection). It is characterized by its frame structure, bit rate, and bandwidth. OTU k capacities are defined for k = 0, 1, 2, 2e, 3, 3e2, and 4 where k indicates the bit rate of the client signa (1.2 Gbit/s, 2.5 Gbit/s, 10.0 Gbit/s, 10.4 Gbit/s, 40.4 Gbit/s, 41.8 Gbit/s, 104.8 Gbit/s).
ODs extract individual wavelengths from the DWDM optical that is generated using an Optical Multiplexer (OM).
A multiplexed optical signal containing multiple wavelengths or channels.
A lightwave transmission system that can multiplex to 8, 16, 80, or more wavelengths, transmit the resulting multiplexed signal, and then demultiplex the signal at the other end.
Used to describe the OADM line, spans, ILAs to the next OADM line.

An instrument that measures the amount of optical power present at the end of a fiber or cable.
An optical card that provides WDM protection.

The ratio (expressed in units of dB) of optical power reflected by a component or an assembly to the optical power incident on a component port when that component or assembly is introduced into a link or system.
The ratio between the optical signal power of the data signal and the power of the optical noise signal.

A designated optical channel used to carry communications related to maintenance and operational functions of the network rather than customer traffic. The OSC supports the following communications: node-to-node, interworking, client LAN, and orderwire communication.
An instrument that locates faults in optical fibers or infers attenuation by backscattered light measurements.

The optical system component that adds or removes a signal from the transmission system – on one side connecting to the client equipment and on the other the line equipment. A standardized method for transparent transport of services over optical wavelengths in DWDM systems, as described in ITU-T G.709.
The OTM is the information structure that is transported across an ONNI. The indexes n and m define the number of supported wavelengths and bit rates at the interface.

The air handling space between walls, under structural floors, and above drop ceilings that can be used to route intrabuilding cabling.
A cable whose flammability and smoke characteristics allow it to be routed in a plenum area without being enclosed in a conduit.
Connection oriented protocol established between two devices that carry packet cards from one point to another.
The direction of the electric field in the lightwave.

Loss of optical power that occurs during the polarization process. Polarized light waves are light waves in which the vibrations occur in a single-plane. The process of transforming unpolarized light into polarized light is known as polarization (the orientation of the electric and magnetic field vectors of a propagating electro-magnetic wave).

Output pulse broadening due to random coupling of the two polarization modes in an optical fiber. PMD is an inherent property of all optical media. It is caused by the difference in the propagation velocities of light in the orthogonal principal polarization states of the transmission medium. The net effect is that if an optical pulse contains both polarization components, then the different polarization components will travel at different speeds and arrive at different times, smearing the received optical signal.

A feature that allows a user to suppress alarm reporting and performance monitoring during provisioning by supporting multiple states (automatic, in-service, and not monitored) for low-speed ports.
Provides rack level power interface and circuit breakers.

The process that the user specifies parameter values for an entity in advance of some of the equipment being present. These parameters are maintained only in NVM. These modifications are initiated locally or remotely by a management system (such as 1830 PSS ZIC for example). Preprovisioning provides for the de-coupling of manual intervention tasks (for example, install cards) from those tasks associated with configuring the node to provide services (for example, specifying the entities to be cross-connected).
The main timing clock reference in SDH equipment.
Refers to the process of detecting degrading conditions not severe enough to initiate protection switching or alarming, but indicative of an impending signal fail or Signal Degrade defect.
Extra capacity (channels, cards) in transmission equipment that is not intended to be used for service, but rather to serve as backup against equipment failures.
To provision traffic to be carried by protection tributaries when the port tributaries are not being used to carry the protected working traffic.
The members of a group and their roles, for example, working protection, line number, and so on.

One of two signals entering a path selector used for path protection switching or dual-ring interworking. The other is the working path. The designations working and protection are provisioned by the user, whereas the terms active path and standby path indicate the current protection state.

When the working unit is currently considered active by the system and that it is carrying traffic. The “active unit state” specifically refers to the receive direction of operation — because protection switching is unidirectional.
Parameter that indicates the protection facilities is currently carrying traffic.

Parameter that indicates a card is ready to perform its intended function. A provisioned card can be active (ACT), in-service (IS), standby (STBY), provisioned out-of-service (POS), or out-of-service (OOS).

Placing and configuring hardware and software required to activate a telecommunications service for a customer. If the equipment is in place, provisioning may consist of creating or modifying a customer record in a database to activate the services.

Random Access Memory Type of computer memory where programs and current data are stored and can be quickly accessed by the processor. When the computer is turned off, RAM loses its data. An optical network element with a configuration that can be changed remotely. The main benefit of this remote reconfigurability is that it reduces Operating Expenditures (OPEX) when operating a DWDM network. OPEX is reduced because the ROADM eases network provisioning and line tuning at both the initial installation and any upgrades (to increase the capacity or reallocate resources to a new demand matrix).
The process of reconstructing a digital signal to eliminate the effects of noise and distortion.

Part of the Section Overhead (SOH) of a STM-1 signal that contains information from the transmission system, used for various management functions such as monitoring transmission quality, detecting failures, managing alarms, data communication channels, and service channels.
Function that generates the Regenerator Section Overhead (RSOH) in the transmit direction and terminates the RSOH in the receive direction.

The ability of a software system performing its required functions under stated conditions for a stated period of time. The probability for an equipment to fulfill its function. Some of the ways that reliability is measured are: MTBF (Mean Time Between Failures) expressed in hours; Availability = (MTBF)/ (MTBF+MTTR)(%) [where MTTR = mean time to restore]; outage in minutes per year; failures per hour; percentage of failures per 1,000 hours.

glossary.definition: RADIUS servers are network devices that authenticate the identity of each user of network services, provides authorization to use the requested service, and create event information for accounting purposes.

RDI signals convey the defect status of the trail signal at the trail destination (that is, at trail termination sink function) back to the trail origin (that is, trail termination source function). This mechanism allows alignment of the near-end and far-end performance monitoring processes.

REI signals contain either the exact or truncated number of error detection code violations detected in the trail signal at the trail termination sink. This information is conveyed to the trail termination source. This mechanism allows alignment of the near-end and far-end performance monitoring processes.

Any Network Element that is connected to the referenced Network Element through either an electrical or optical link. It may be the adjacent node on a ring, or N nodes away from the reference. It also may be at the same physical location but is usually at another (remote) site.
Provides statistics for remote performance monitoring. Defined in standard RFC 2819.
A receiver and transmitter set designed to amplify attenuated signals. Repeaters are used to extend operating range. See “In-Line Amplifier” (p. 1606) for related term.
A document that describes the specifications of a technology. RFCs are used by the Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF) and other standards bodies.

Counts down the time (in minutes) during which the switch waits to let the worker line recover before switching back to it. This option can be set to prevent the protection switch continually switching if a line has a continual transient fault.

A protection switching mode that after a protection switch occurs, the equipment returns to the nominal configuration (that is, the working equipment is active, and the protection equipment is standby) after any failure conditions that caused a protection switch to occur, clear, or after any external switch commands are reset.

In revertive switching, there is a working and protection high-speed line, card, and so on. When a protection switch occurs, the protection line, card, and so on is selected. When the fault clears, service “reverts” to the working line.
Cable that contains many fibers embedded in a plastic material in parallel, forming a flat ribbon-like structure.

A configuration of nodes comprised of network elements connected in a circular fashion. Under normal conditions, each node is interconnected with its neighbor and includes capacity for transmission in either direction between adjacent nodes. Path switched rings use a head-end bridge and tail-end switch. Line switched rings actively reroute traffic over the protection capacity.

The time taken to make a transition from one state to another, usually measured between the 10% and 90% completion points of the transition. Alternatively, the rise time may be specified at the 20% and 80% amplitudes. Shorter or faster rise times require more bandwidth in a transmission channel.
Registered jack, standardized according to IEC60603-7 .

An interface between two networks. While routers are similar to bridges, they work differently. Routers provide more functionality than bridges. Routers also provide network management capabilities such as load balancing, partitioning of the network, and trouble-shooting.

The change of direction of light rays or photons after striking small particles. It may also be regarded as the diffusion of a light beam caused by the inhomogeneity of the transmitting material.

A timing device (equipment) used to synchronize network equipment that operates according to the principles governed by SDH.
The portion of a transmission facility, including terminating points, between a terminal network element and a line-terminating network element, or two line-terminating network elements.

Capacity added to either an AU-4 or assembly of AU-3s to create an STM-1. Contains always STM-1 framing and optionally maintenance and operational functions. SOH can be subdivided in MSOH (multiplex section overhead) and RSOH (regenerator section overhead).

Secure Shell, a cryptographic network protocol, is used to operate network services securely over an unsecured network Any network service can be secured with SSH, but typical applications include remote command-line login and remote command execution.
Protocol that ensures data security between a server and a client by using encryption.
A pair of OSP fibers connecting two sites.
A network’s ability to automatically recover from the failure of one or more of its components.
Safety extra low voltage.

Computer in a computer network that performs dedicated main tasks that generally require sufficient performance.

A contract between a network service provider and a customer that specifies, usually in measurable terms, what services the network service provider will provide.
Within the 1830 PSS system, services can be of fered directly to end customers or be used internally to a network as transport infrastructure.
This performance monitoring parameter is a second in which a signal failure occurs, or more than a preset amount of coding violations (dependent on the type of signal) occurs.

A survivable, closed loop transport architecture that protects against cable cuts and node failures by providing duplicate, geographically diverse paths for each service. Adjacent nodes on the ring are interconnected using a single pair of optical fibers. One fiber transports traffic in one direction (for example, clockwise), while the second fiber transports traffic in the opposite direction (for example, counterclockwise). In a UPSR, the source node bridges its outgoing traffic along opposite directions around the ring (on paths provided by SONET synchronous transport channels). In contrast to BLSR, a UPSR: • is path-specific as opposed to line specific • does not allow extra traffic (because traffic is bridged) • requires less coordination from source to destination (because the destination network element can make all its decisions without involving the source)

A minimal, datagram-oriented, transport network protocol above the IP network layer that does not guarantee data ordering or delivery. Because it is datagram-oriented, each send operation by the application results in the transmission of a single IP datagram. This contrasts with the Transmission Control Protocol (TCP) that is byte stream oriented and guarantees the delivery and ordering of the bytes sent. Because it is a byte stream oriented, a single send operation may result in a no IP datagrams (buffering), a single IP datagram, or multiple IP datagrams.
